summary: After the 2013 decision to make XML the canonical RFC format, plain-text renderings still matter for readability and archival. This informational document gives the requirements for the plain-text RFC format, building on the higher-level requirements in RFC 6949.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7994 sets requirements for plain-text versions of RFCs rendered from XML. It describes how text should be encoded, paginated, and laid out.

subtitle: Requirements for plain-text renderings of RFCs generated from XML source.

tldr.problem: XML became the canonical RFC format, but plain text remained important to readers and tools, so its rendered form needed requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies UTF-8 encoding, ASCII-only artwork, pagination, line width, line endings, spacing, and the relationship to the XML source.
tldr.outcome: The requirements apply to RFCs published after the format transition. RFC 7994 has been updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7994 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 9920. Its requirements apply to plain-text RFCs published after the format transition.

sections.title: Why Plain Text Remains a Publication Format
sections.content:
In 2013, the RFC Series moved from plain text as the canonical format to XML as the canonical source, with human-readable formats rendered from XML. Plain text remained important to readers and existing tools, so RFC 7994 sets requirements for that publication format.

The requirements do not apply to plain-text RFCs published before the transition. The RFC also notes that details may change as publication tools are completed and that future changes may not be backwards-compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: XML is the source used to create RFCs, but people still use plain-text versions. This document sets rules for producing those text versions.

sections.title: Character Encoding and Artwork
sections.content:
Plain-text RFC files use UTF-8 and include a Byte Order Mark to identify the encoding. Non-ASCII characters are allowed only in a limited and controlled way, with ASCII equivalents rendered according to the referenced guidance.

The text format includes ASCII art. If the XML source contains artwork that is not ASCII art, the text output must point readers to the corresponding figure in the HTML version. If two publication formats conflict, the RFC advises readers to review the XML and PDF.
sections.plainLanguage: The text file uses UTF-8 and marks that encoding at the start. It can include diagrams made from ASCII characters; other figures need a pointer to the HTML version.

sections.title: Page and Line Layout
sections.content:
The publication process creates one plain-text output with basic pagination. A form feed appears at most every 58 lines, including blank lines. A script or instructions are to be made available for readers who want to remove pagination.

Lines are limited to 72 characters, including indentation, followed by CR LF. Paragraphs are single-spaced with one blank line between them. The table of contents lists section numbers and titles without page numbers, and running headers and footers are not added.
sections.plainLanguage: Pages and lines have length limits. Paragraphs have a blank line between them, and the text does not repeat a running title at the top or bottom of each page.

sections.title: Rendering from the XML Source
sections.content:
The plain-text formatter uses elements from the xml2rfc version 3 source vocabulary. It builds the text according to the RFC Style Guide and the related guidance cited by the document.

The RFC explains that earlier tools and practices for converting xml2rfc version 2 into text inform the version 3 conversion. It highlights encoding, page layout, figures, artwork, and pagination as areas that need attention.
sections.plainLanguage: A formatter reads the XML source and produces the text version. It follows the RFC style rules for structure and layout.

sections.title: Preserving the Source Meaning
sections.content: The format requirements themselves involve no significant security considerations. The RFC warns that an unintended change during conversion from XML to text could corrupt a standard, practice, or critical protocol information.
sections.plainLanguage: The main concern is that conversion could change important text by mistake. Such a change could alter the meaning of a protocol rule.
